questions.stem: An events coordinator is staffing a trade-show booth. She has pasted the printed session schedule into a Claude chat, and visitors ask her short, simple questions such as 'When does the keynote start?' or 'Which room is the data-privacy panel in?'. Answers must come back almost instantly so the line keeps moving. Which model tier is the BEST fit for this job?

options.text: Opus, because visitors expect every answer to be correct and Opus is the most capable model of the three tiers.
Haiku, because the questions are simple lookups in text she already pasted and the work depends on very fast replies.
Sonnet with extended thinking turned on, so it double-checks each answer against the schedule before replying.
Rotate between all three tiers during the day so she can find out which one visitors seem to like the most.

questions.explanation: The cues are **simple** questions, answers already in text she supplied, and **speed** because people are waiting. Haiku is the fastest, lowest-cost tier, and the exam guide's own guidance points faster, lower-cost models at straightforward, high-volume work while reserving the most capable model for complex reasoning. Looking up a time in a pasted schedule needs no deep reasoning, so the lightest tier meets the quality bar with the least delay.

whyWrong.A: Opus is the slowest of the three tiers. Its extra reasoning adds nothing to a lookup in text she already pasted, and the delay is exactly what she needs to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Adding step-by-step checking to trivial lookups makes every reply slower without making it more accurate; the schedule is already in the chat.
whyWrong.D: Rotating models to see which one visitors prefer is not a selection method. The task cues (simple, fast) already point clearly to the fastest tier.

questions.mindset: Simple + someone waiting = the fastest tier that meets the bar.

questions.stem: A data team's internal wiki page, written two years ago, says: 'Always use Opus for analysis work. Sonnet is the weaker model.' Since then a new Sonnet version has been released, and the team's workspace now offers this new Sonnet alongside an older Opus version. An analyst wants to pick the model for a recurring monthly churn analysis. What is the MOST sound way for her to decide?

options.text: Follow the wiki, because Opus is always the stronger family and a Sonnet model can never match an Opus model at analysis.
Choose whichever model was released most recently, because newer releases are the safe default for recurring analysis work.
Ask Claude in a chat which of the two models is smarter and then use whichever one the answer recommends for the work.
Treat tier names as positions within one generation, then run both models on a few past months' data and compare results.

questions.explanation: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus describe **relative position within a generation**: lighter tiers are faster and cheaper, heavier tiers are more capable. Across generations the ordering is not guaranteed — a newer mid-tier model can match or beat an older top-tier one — so a two-year-old 'always Opus' rule may be out of date. The reliable way to decide is to **test both models on real past work** (same task, same data) and compare accuracy, quality and edge cases before standardizing.

whyWrong.A: This treats tier names as a permanent ranking. Model versions change often, and a newer mid-tier model can match or outperform an older top-tier one.
whyWrong.B: 'Newest wins' is just as untested as 'Opus wins.' Release date alone does not tell her which model handles her specific analysis best.
whyWrong.C: A model's opinion about which model is smarter is not evidence — self-reports are not a reliable quality signal. Running both on real past data is the comparison that actually shows quality.

questions.mindset: Tier names rank models within a generation, not forever; test on your real work.

questions.stem: A legal-operations specialist usually works with Haiku because it is fast for her quick tasks. Now she wants Claude to consider a very large set of supplier agreements together in a single pass, totalling well over 150,000 words, so it can spot clauses that conflict across contracts. Before she starts, which difference between the model tiers is MOST important for her to check?

options.text: Current Sonnet and Opus models list a much larger context window than Haiku, so a very large set may not fit in one pass on Haiku.
Haiku reads text faster than the other tiers, so it can take in a larger set of documents in one pass than Sonnet or Opus can.
All current tiers share the same context window, so the only differences she needs to weigh are response speed and cost.
Haiku has no limit on how much text it reads; it only gives shorter answers, so she should ask it for a more detailed reply.

questions.explanation: The **context window** is how much text a model can consider at once, and it differs by model. At the time of writing, current Sonnet and Opus models list a window of **1 million tokens**, while current Haiku lists **200K tokens** — roughly 150,000 words. A set totalling well over 150,000 words will not fit in Haiku's window in a single pass, so she needs a model whose window can hold the whole set (or a plan to split the work). Spotting clauses that interact **across** contracts also favours a more capable tier.

whyWrong.B: Speed has nothing to do with capacity. A faster model does not get a larger context window.
whyWrong.C: Current models list different context window sizes — about 1M tokens for current Sonnet and Opus versus 200K for Haiku — so 'all tiers share the same window' is factually wrong.
whyWrong.D: Every model has a context window limit, and asking for a longer answer changes the output length, not how much input fits.

questions.mindset: Check that the model can hold the whole job before judging its speed or quality.

questions.stem: A marketing lead asks Claude about advertising rules a regulator announced last month. The answer describes the old rules and does not mention the change. A colleague says: 'You were on Haiku. Switch to Opus; the bigger model knows more recent news.' What is the BEST advice?

options.text: Agree with the colleague, because the most capable tier is trained on the most recent data and will know about last month's rules.
Stay on Haiku, because the fastest tier is updated most often and has the newest knowledge of any of the three model tiers.
Explain that every model has a knowledge cutoff, so she should use web search or research mode and then verify against the regulator's publication.
Ask the same model to answer again as of today's date, which makes it switch from its training data to current information.

questions.explanation: Every Claude model's knowledge comes from training data that stops at a **cutoff date**, and no tier escapes that. A change announced last month is likely beyond any current model's training, whatever its tier. Switching models does not solve this. The fix is to give Claude **web search or research mode** so it works from current sources, then verify the key points against the regulator's own publication — the same diligence that applies before sharing any AI output bound for a compliance audience.

whyWrong.A: A more capable tier reasons better, but that does not give it knowledge after its cutoff. Recency is a separate property, and tier does not guarantee it.
whyWrong.B: Speed has nothing to do with how recent a model's knowledge is. Every tier's knowledge stops at its training cutoff; being faster does not make Haiku's data newer.
whyWrong.D: Telling the model today's date does not give it new information. Without a search tool it can only guess, and that risks a hallucinated answer.

questions.mindset: Capability and recency are different; for current facts, give Claude a search tool and verify.

questions.stem: A people-operations manager with no technical background asks you for a one-sentence explanation of Claude's model options so she can tell her team which one to pick. Which explanation is the MOST accurate?

options.text: Haiku is meant for short texts and Opus for long texts. Sonnet sits in the middle, so pick a model based on how long the document is.
Each tier specializes in a subject: Haiku for creative writing, Sonnet for business documents, and Opus for technical and coding work.
All three tiers are equally intelligent and give the same quality of answers; the only real difference between them is the price.
Haiku is fastest and cheapest, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence, and Opus is the most capable of the three but slower and costlier.

questions.explanation: The tiers are a **trade-off between capability, speed and cost**. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest, Sonnet is the balanced combination of speed and intelligence, and Opus is the most capable of the three for complex reasoning, but slower and more expensive per request. Choose the tier by how hard the task is and how fast and cheap it must be — not by subject or length.

whyWrong.A: Document length alone is not the dividing line. A long but simple task can suit a lighter model, and a short but subtle one can need Opus.
whyWrong.B: The names sound literary, but the tiers are not subject specialists. Each one handles writing, business and technical work at a different level of capability.
whyWrong.C: The tiers differ in capability as well as cost and speed. That difference is the reason the choice matters.

questions.mindset: Tiers trade capability against speed and cost, not subjects or document length.

questions.stem: A department head proposes that everyone on her team should use Opus for every task 'to be safe'. Most of the team's daily work is quick email rewrites, short summaries and tagging inbound requests. A few times a month someone does a deep competitive analysis. The team already runs out of its Claude usage allowance by mid-week. What should you recommend?

options.text: Keep Opus for everything, but ask the team to write shorter prompts so each Opus request uses less of the shared allowance.
Move the whole team to Haiku for every task, because it is the cheapest tier and will stretch the usage allowance the furthest.
Use a lighter or balanced tier for routine rewrites, summaries and tagging, and reserve Opus for the deep competitive analyses.
Upgrade every seat to a higher plan, so the team can keep using Opus on every task without having to think about its limits.

questions.explanation: Using the most capable tier for quick rewrites and tagging spends budget and time on work a lighter tier does just as well: heavier models cost more per request and respond more slowly, and the exam guide's own sample rationale rejects always using the top model as a waste of both cost and latency budget. Match the tier to the task: lighter or balanced models for routine work, Opus for the few analyses that need deep reasoning.

whyWrong.A: Shorter prompts save a little, but they don't fix the real mismatch: a heavy model doing light work all day.
whyWrong.B: This overcorrects. The occasional deep competitive analysis needs strong multi-step reasoning, and using the cheapest tier for it risks weak results and rework.
whyWrong.D: Spending more money to avoid making a choice is the overkill pattern. Matching tiers to tasks solves the problem at no extra cost.

questions.mindset: Using the biggest model for everything is not safety; it wastes speed and budget.

questions.stem: A policy analyst asks Haiku to compare three draft remote-work policies against the company's employment-law obligations and its union agreement. Her prompt is already clear: it gives the context, the criteria and the output format she wants. The response lists surface differences but misses two places where clauses in different policies interact and create a conflict. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Ask Haiku in the same chat to check its own answer for mistakes and to confirm that it found all the conflicts this time.
Rerun the same prompt on Opus, since the task needs multi-step reasoning across interacting clauses, then have HR review the result.
Add three more example conflicts to the Haiku prompt, run it several times, and keep whichever conflicts come up most often.
Paste each of the three policies into its own separate chat, so Haiku can concentrate on a single policy at a time.

questions.explanation: The prompt is already clear, so the remaining gap is **capability**: finding conflicts that only appear when clauses are weighed against each other is the nuanced, multi-step reasoning that belongs to the most capable tier, which is exactly what the exam guide reserves it for. Moving up a tier is the right lever here. Because the result touches legal and union obligations, a human review is still required before anyone acts on it.

whyWrong.A: Asking the same model to grade its own work rarely surfaces reasoning it could not do the first time. The capability gap stays.
whyWrong.C: Examples mainly fix format and consistency problems. The missed conflicts are novel clause interactions that no example can list in advance, and a majority vote cannot confirm completeness.
whyWrong.D: Splitting the policies apart removes the cross-policy view the task needs. Conflicts between policies cannot be found one policy at a time.

questions.mindset: When the prompt is already good and the task is nuanced, the lever is a more capable tier.

questions.stem: An e-commerce coordinator wants to turn about 2,000 product reviews a month into a fixed set of fields: product, sentiment, main complaint and whether a refund is mentioned. A colleague insists: 'Haiku is only for toy tasks. For anything real we need Opus.' Which response is BEST?

options.text: Explain that Haiku is built for fast, high-volume work, so start with it, test a real sample, and move up only if it falls short.
Agree with the colleague, because extracting fields from reviews is real business work and only the Opus tier is suitable for it.
Run half of the reviews through Sonnet and half through Opus for a full month, then compare which half of the results looks better.
Point out that Haiku is available only to developers using the API, so the team could not use it in the Claude app anyway.

questions.explanation: Haiku is the fastest, lowest-cost tier, and the exam guide's guidance points faster, lower-cost models at **straightforward, high-volume** work. Extracting a fixed set of fields from short reviews is well defined and repetitive — exactly that shape. The right move is to start with the lighter model, **test it on a real sample** of actual reviews, and step up a tier only if it misses the quality bar.

whyWrong.B: This dismisses Haiku based on reputation instead of testing. For well-defined extraction at volume, the most capable tier usually adds cost and delay without a quality gain.
whyWrong.C: A month-long split test between the two more expensive tiers skips the lightest plausible option, and it costs a full month of output to answer something a small sample could.
whyWrong.D: This is not true: Haiku is not developer-only, and availability in Claude's apps depends on plan and organization settings. It is a made-up reason to rule out a valid option.

questions.mindset: Lighter does not mean toy: test the cheapest plausible tier on real samples first.

questions.stem: A team lead is preparing a short briefing to help colleagues choose between Claude's model tiers. Which TWO statements are accurate to include? Choose TWO.

options.text: Opus generally takes longer to respond than Haiku, so the most capable tier is not the best choice when someone is waiting.
Tier names are a permanent ranking: any Opus model will outperform any Sonnet model, whichever versions are being compared.
Haiku is the tier that Anthropic describes as the best combination of speed and intelligence for everyday work.
Moving the same task from Haiku to Opus usually costs more, whether in API pricing or in how much usage allowance it consumes.
Only the Opus tier can read images and charts, so any task that includes a screenshot needs to go to Opus.

questions.explanation: Two properties change predictably across the tiers. **Speed**: heavier models respond more slowly than Haiku, and the top model's extra capability is wasted latency when someone is waiting on a reply. **Cost**: heavier models carry higher per-token prices, and in the Claude apps heavier models consume usage limits faster. Both facts help colleagues make the trade-off consciously.

whyWrong.B: Tier names show position within one generation. A newer Sonnet can match or beat an older Opus, so 'any Opus beats any Sonnet' is false.
whyWrong.C: 'Best combination of speed and intelligence' is how the balanced middle tier, Sonnet, is described. Haiku is described as the fastest.
whyWrong.E: All current Claude models support image input (vision), so a screenshot does not by itself require Opus.

questions.mindset: Learn the trade-off pattern (speed vs capability vs cost), not myths about the tiers.

questions.stem: A product research team has 600 anonymized customer-interview transcripts. Step 1 is to tag each transcript's mentions of pricing, onboarding and support. Step 2 is to synthesize the patterns across all the tagged excerpts into a strategy memo for executives, weighing trade-offs between three possible product investments. Which TWO model choices BEST fit this workflow? Choose TWO.

options.text: Use Opus for the tagging step, because a tagging mistake on any transcript could spread into the executive memo later.
Use Haiku for the tagging step, after checking a sample of its tags to confirm it meets the quality bar for this team.
Use Haiku for the synthesis step as well, since by that stage it only has to summarize tags that already exist.
Pick one model for both steps so that the results stay consistent, and choose that model based on the harder step.
Use Opus for the synthesis memo, since weighing trade-offs between investments needs nuanced multi-step reasoning.

questions.explanation: One workflow can use **more than one tier**. Tagging 600 transcripts against three fixed categories is high-volume and well defined, which suits the fastest, lowest-cost tier — with a sample check on real transcripts as the quality gate. The synthesis step is low-volume but high-stakes judgment, which is where the most capable tier earns its cost. Testing each step's output on real data is what makes the split safe.

whyWrong.A: A sample check already covers tagging quality. Running Opus across all 600 transcripts adds cost and time to the easy part of the job.
whyWrong.C: Synthesis is not simple summarizing. It means weighing trade-offs between investments for executives, which is exactly the nuanced reasoning that needs a stronger tier.
whyWrong.D: Using one model for the sake of consistency means overpaying for the bulk step or under-powering the judgment step. Matching each step is more efficient.

questions.mindset: Split the workflow: light tier for bulk steps, strong tier for the judgment step.

questions.stem: A small marketing agency wants to set one default Claude model for its staff. Daily work is drafting client emails, summarizing call notes and light analysis of campaign spreadsheets. A few times a quarter, a strategist builds a complex multi-market positioning plan. Which default is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Make Sonnet the default for the everyday drafting and analysis, and tell staff to switch to Opus for the complex positioning plans.
Make Opus the default for everyone, because client work deserves the most capable model even when the task is a quick email.
Make Haiku the default for everyone, because most of the team's tasks are short and the cheapest tier saves the most budget.
Set no default at all and let each person pick whatever model they like, because individual preference matters most here.

questions.explanation: Sonnet is the tier that **balances speed and intelligence**, aimed at everyday work such as content creation and data analysis — which fits the agency's daily mix. The occasional complex, multi-market plan is the exception that justifies switching up to Opus. A sensible default plus a clear rule for when to switch beats one model for everything.

whyWrong.B: Opus for every quick email adds delay and uses up the allowance faster, with no real quality gain on routine drafting.
whyWrong.C: Haiku may handle some short tasks well, but making it the default for the spreadsheet analysis and client-facing drafts risks quality, and it gives no guidance for the complex plans.
whyWrong.D: With no guidance, people tend to drift to the biggest or the most familiar model. A default with a switching rule gives better results at the right cost.

questions.mindset: Balanced tier as the everyday default; step up only for genuinely complex work.

questions.stem: A team is writing a quick guide to help colleagues decide when a task should go to Opus instead of Haiku. Which TWO cues in a task description MOST strongly point to Opus? Choose TWO.

options.text: The task requires reasoning across many interdependent constraints, where one weak step would undermine the whole result.
The task involves thousands of short items that each need the same simple label from a fixed list of categories.
A mistake would be costly and the task runs only occasionally, so accuracy matters far more than speed or cost.
The final output will be a long document, so it needs the model that is able to write the most words in one reply.
A colleague is waiting in real time for each answer, so the reply needs to arrive as quickly as possible.

questions.explanation: The strongest cues for the most capable tier are **difficulty** (reasoning across many interdependent constraints, where one weak step undermines the whole result) and **stakes at low volume** (a costly mistake on an occasional task, where accuracy matters far more than speed or cost). Volume, output length and real-time waiting all point toward the lighter tier instead.

whyWrong.B: High volume, simple and repetitive is the classic cue for the fastest, lowest-cost tier.
whyWrong.D: Length alone is not a capability cue. A long but straightforward document can come from a lighter tier, so choose by difficulty, not word count.
whyWrong.E: Real-time waiting points toward faster tiers. Opus is slower, so latency is a reason to look lighter.

questions.mindset: Pick Opus for difficulty and stakes, not for volume, speed or length.

questions.stem: A sales rep uses Claude during live video calls to quickly rephrase technical answers in plain language for customers. On Opus, responses arrive noticeably later than on lighter tiers, which causes awkward pauses. In a side-by-side test of 20 past rephrasings, Haiku and Sonnet produced equally good results. After each call she also writes a detailed tailored proposal that weighs the customer's constraints. Which TWO changes BEST fit? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep using Opus during calls, but type shorter prompts so that each response comes back faster.
Use a faster tier such as Haiku or Sonnet for the in-call rephrasing, since tests showed equal quality.
Tell Opus at the start of each chat to respond as quickly as it possibly can during the live calls.
Keep Opus for the post-call proposals, where weighing the customer's constraints benefits from deeper reasoning.
Stop using Claude during live calls and do all the rephrasing by hand, so that there are never any pauses.

questions.explanation: Her own test settles the in-call question: the lighter tiers matched quality on short rephrasings, and switching to a smaller, faster model is one of the primary documented levers for cutting latency, so they remove the pauses at no cost in quality. The post-call proposal is a different task — tailored and multi-factor, with no one waiting — which suits the most capable tier. Choose per task, not per person.

whyWrong.A: Prompt length has only a small effect on how fast a heavy model responds, and her test already showed a faster tier meets the quality bar. The tier is the real lever.
whyWrong.C: Telling a model to hurry does not change how fast it generates. Model choice and output length are the real levers, and the lighter tiers already matched quality in her test.
whyWrong.E: Giving up on a useful tool because of a solvable speed issue is the escape-hatch distractor. Switching tiers fixes the pauses.

questions.mindset: Match the tier to each task: speed where someone is waiting, depth where the stakes are.

questions.stem: An operations manager wants Claude to carry a long, multi-step piece of work through to a finished result in one session: reconcile figures across a large workbook with many tabs, explain each discrepancy it finds, and then draft a finished summary report for the leadership team. Errors early in the chain would carry through to the final report. Which model tier is the MOST appropriate starting point?

options.text: Haiku, because a long job with many steps finishes sooner on the fastest tier, which matters most when there is a lot of work.
Sonnet for the first half of the job, then switch to Haiku once the reconciliation is done, to save on the remaining cost.
Opus, because long multi-step work where early errors carry forward calls for the most capable of the three tiers.
Whichever tier is selected by default, since model choice matters for single questions but not for long multi-step work.

questions.explanation: In a long chain, an early reasoning slip spreads into everything downstream — the reconciliation, the explanations and the final report — so **capability matters more than speed**. Multi-step, nuanced, error-compounding work is exactly what the most capable tier is reserved for; optimize for speed or cost later, once accuracy is secured.

whyWrong.A: Finishing sooner does not help if the reconciliation is wrong. In a long dependent chain, a weaker step costs more in rework than speed saves.
whyWrong.B: Dropping to the lightest tier for the final leadership report weakens the step whose quality matters most to readers, and switching tiers mid-chain adds inconsistency risk.
whyWrong.D: Model choice matters more on long multi-step work, not less, because errors compound across steps.

questions.mindset: Long chains magnify early mistakes; give them the most capable tier.

questions.stem: A finance team switched to Haiku to draft the quarterly variance commentary for the board pack. The drafts arrive quickly, but reviewers now spend several hours each quarter rewriting the explanations of why variances occurred, because the reasoning is thin. The manager says the switch was a success because Haiku is the cheapest tier. What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: Keep Haiku but add two more reviewers, since the model cost savings are larger than the cost of the extra review hours.
Count the rework in the cost: test a more capable tier on last quarter's data and compare drafting cost plus review time.
Keep Haiku and ask it to write longer explanations, because the problem is that the commentary is too brief for the board.
Move every finance task to Opus, including routine invoice tagging, so that thin reasoning can never happen again.

questions.explanation: The cheapest tier per request is not the cheapest overall when it fails the quality bar and creates **rework**. Board-facing variance commentary is low-volume analytical writing that needs real causal reasoning, which suits a more capable tier. The disciplined move is to **test a more capable tier on last quarter's actual data** and compare total effort — drafting cost plus review hours — before settling on the default.

whyWrong.A: Adding reviewers locks in the rework instead of removing its cause, and no one has checked that the savings actually exceed the cost of the review hours.
whyWrong.C: Longer is not deeper. Thin causal reasoning padded with more words still needs rewriting.
whyWrong.D: This overcorrects. Routine invoice tagging is a high-volume, simple task where a lighter tier is the right fit.

questions.mindset: True cost = model cost + human rework; cheapest per request can be most expensive overall.
